subject: history
title: The Columbian Exchange and Colonial Labour
welcome_lead: Trace plants, animals, microbes and people moving across the Atlantic — and the systems of labour built upon them.
meta_desc: History Conquest of the Americas Adventure 3: Columbian Exchange, encomienda, repartimiento and Atlantic slavery.
final_note: You have surveyed the biological and human consequences of conquest. The colonial Americas were forged in exchange and exploitation.

walkthroughs.body_html: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, tobacco and capsicums moved from the Americas to Europe and beyond, while wheat, sugarcane, citrus, horses, pigs and cattle moved west. Old World diseases — smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus — devastated Indigenous populations who lacked immunity, contributing to demographic collapse of up to 90% in some regions.

The encomienda granted conquistadors rights to Indigenous tribute and labour. Abuses prompted reform attempts, including the Laws of Burgos (1512) and the New Laws (1542). Repartimiento and the Andean mita provided rotational labour, particularly for silver mining at Potosí from 1545. African enslaved labour grew rapidly in the Caribbean and Brazil.

Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas reshaped global trade, financing European wars and the Asian silk and spice trades via Manila. New crops contributed to population growth in Eurasia. The trade in enslaved Africans — over twelve million people forcibly shipped across the Atlantic — underpinned plantation economies and remains a defining injustice of the early modern world.
